title: Division plane depends on the ratio of growth rate to division frequency

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Division plane depends on the ratio of growth rate to division frequency

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A growing cell divides according to the shape it has reached, set by the ratio of its growth rate to its division frequency: if markedly oblong it divides transversely, if a little more than a hemisphere obliquely, and if less than a hemisphere by a vertical wall along its axis.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the manner in which this latter cell divides will simply depend upon the form it has assumed before each successive act of division takes place, that is to say upon the ratio between its rate of growth and the frequency of its successive divisions.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter VIII, “The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)”; topic “Growth rate and plane of division”. Scope: apical and growing cells of mosses, liverworts, ferns and algae

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch08-16: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: All variables can be extracted from sufficiently long time-lapse sequences and the orientation regimes are explicit. Existing datasets permit tests in restricted taxa, but not the full cryptogam scope or a clean causal attribution.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate each apical cell's growth rate, interdivision interval, pre-division shape, and wall orientation, then test whether the growth-to-division ratio predicts the stated transverse, oblique, and axial regimes.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Polarity and tissue stress may confound the growth-rate ratio.

Suitable apical-cell series for mosses, liverworts, ferns, and algae are limited.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The shape-to-plane mapping is measurable and overlaps rules that public embryo and meristem volumes were built to study. Those volumes are the wrong taxa for the apical cells named in the claim, so they test a proxy. The growth-rate clause adds little beyond the shape already observed, which caps how decisive a confirmation can be.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Record cell shape immediately before division and the plane that is used: transverse in markedly oblong cells, oblique when the cell is a little more than a hemisphere, and longitudinal when it is less than a hemisphere. That mapping, in cells whose shape was set by the growth-to-division interval, would support the claim; planes uncorrelated with those shape classes would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Shape is partly defined by the growth-to-division ratio, so that half of the wording is close to a description of the cell that is about to divide.

The three-way rule was stated for moss, liverwort, fern and algal apical cells, which these Arabidopsis volumes only approximate.
